Based on my web search, I found information about the NeurIPS 2026 author guidelines for heading and paragraph formatting. Here's what I found:

## Heading Formatting Styles

All headings should be lower case (except for first word and proper nouns), flush left, and bold.

For the specific heading levels:

- First-level headings should be in 12-point type.
- Second-level headings should be in 10-point type. Third-level headings should be in 10-point type.

For deeper structural elements, there is also a \paragraph command available, which sets the heading in bold, flush left, and inline with the text, with the heading followed by 1 em of space. This would be used for subsubsections or fourth-level headings.

## Paragraph Formatting

Paragraphs are separated by 1/2 line space (5.5 points), with no indentation.

## General Formatting Requirements

Use 10 point type with a vertical spacing (leading) of 11 points. Times New Roman is the preferred typeface throughout, and will be selected for you by default.

NeurIPS 2026 has no rule either way; both forms are explicitly legal. The official template (page 2 of the formatting instructions) demonstrates all three options side-by-side in Section 3 "Headings": numbered first/second/third-level, plus the inline `\paragraph` form. They're shown as equivalent stylistic choices, not a hierarchy of preference. There's no requirement to use or avoid `4.2.1`-style numbering.

**Practical recommendation: keep `\subsubsection*` (your current state).** Numbered subsubsections are unusual in NeurIPS papers — most use either the unnumbered starred form or `\paragraph{}` for inline bold runs (which you already use at lines 1061/1063/1065/1076 for "Backbone specifications.", "Training hyperparameters.", etc.). Switching to numbered `4.2.1–4.2.4` would:
- add visual clutter and a small amount of vertical space (you're already over 9 pages per `todo.md`)
- only pay off if you need to `\ref` them from elsewhere in the body — `\subsubsection*` can't be cross-referenced

Switch to numbered only if you find yourself wanting to write "see §4.2.3"; otherwise the current `\subsubsection*` is the right call. If you want to reclaim a bit more space, downgrade them to `\paragraph{Diagnosis.}` etc. — that's the most compact option and matches the rest of §4.

Sources:
- [Formatting Instructions For NeurIPS 2026 (PDF, p.2 §3 Headings)](http://web.uvic.ca/~nmehta/incentives_and_machine_learning_spring2026/neurips_2026.pdf)
- [NeurIPS 2026 Style Files](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2026/PaperInformation/StyleFiles)

61	\section{Introduction}
62	\label{sec:intro}
63	
64	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, observability-domain TSFMs deployed at scale~\citep{cohen2025toto}, and continuous flow-matching forecasters such as Sundial~\citep{liu2025sundial} that bypass tokenization entirely. A parallel adaptation route reprograms pretrained LLMs as forecasters: Time-LLM~\citep{jin2024timellm} reprograms patch embeddings into the LLM token space, GPT4TS~\citep{zhou2023onefitsall} freezes the LLM's transformer blocks and tunes only positional and layer-norm parameters, AutoTimes~\citep{liu2024autotimes} casts forecasting as autoregressive next-token prediction, S$^2$IP-LLM~\citep{pan2024s2ipllm} attaches semantic prompts derived from the LLM's own embedding space, and UniTime~\citep{liu2024unitime} unifies cross-domain forecasting via natural-language domain instructions. Recent designs push toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.
65	
66	Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a) -- flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes (quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes), and instance normalization handles only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) is encoded in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses of MOMENT and related TSFMs have reported~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).
67	
68	This natural mixture-of-experts approach fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization once any backbone layers are unfrozen (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}b). When the AdaMix-style adapter pool~\citep{wang2022adamix} is combined with a learned hidden-state softmax router and Switch-style load balancing~\citep{fedus2022switch}, and applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to zero in most unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The router learns to send every window to the same expert, and the remaining experts are never used. The mechanism is what we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes (formalized in Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}; signal-ratio diagnostic in Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}), leaving it with homogenized hidden states. Even with the backbone frozen, hidden-state routing still underperforms; with the backbone unfrozen, the dominant expert receives larger gradients which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, closing a co-adaptation feedback loop within tens of training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
69	
70	The failure is specific to learnable-affine instance normalization placed inside the encoder pipeline. Backbones such as Moirai, which apply only non-learnable per-instance I/O scaling and use RMSNorm internally (rather than RevIN-style learnable-affine normalization upstream of the encoder), do not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}), and standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) recover at most $10.9\%$ MSE, still $2.7\times$ worse than RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), because the problem lies in the router's \emph{input}, not its optimization.
71	
72	Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is direct. \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen; only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so within a fixed MoE architecture frozen should match or beat unfrozen, which we confirm empirically (frozen best on $4/6$, unfrozen-wins bounded at $\leq 13\%$).
73	
74	\paragraph{Contributions.}
75	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=0.15em, topsep=0.2em]
76	\item We identify \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: an architectural failure mode of MoE adapters on instance-normalized TSFMs that is upstream of the optimization-induced collapses targeted by Switch~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, ReMoE~\citep{wang2025remoe}, and Expert-Choice~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}. Eight causal controls (RevIN ablation, BatchNorm/GroupNorm swaps, router-input interpolation, vision cross-modality, and others) converge on the normalizer as cause.
77	\item We formalize the mechanism via a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) and derive a tractable signal-ratio predictor $R(\mathcal{D})$ that anticipates which datasets benefit from raw routing at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$), including boundary cases where it correctly does not (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). The predictor generalizes across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.
78	\item We propose RR-MoA, the \textbf{minimal causal intervention}: changing only the router's input from normalized hidden states to $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$, with no change to the optimizer, the experts, or the frozen backbone. RR-MoA wins $54/54$ cells against AdaMix (the same architecture with collapsed routing), strictly dominates $11$ optimization-side rescue mechanisms ($720$ runs; best rescue recovers $\leq 10.9\%$, RR-MoA $2.7{\times}$ better), and is not subsumed by naive $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection ($+42$--$239\%$ MSE; $11/18$ cells re-collapse). 79	\end{itemize}

Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

+Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, observability-domain deployments~\citep{cohen2025toto}, tokenization-free flow-matching forecasters~\citep{liu2025sundial}, and a parallel route that reprograms pretrained LLMs as forecasters via patch-to-token reprogramming~\citep{jin2024timellm}, layer-norm-only tuning~\citep{zhou2023onefitsall}, autoregressive next-token forecasting~\citep{liu2024autotimes}, semantic prompts~\citep{pan2024s2ipllm}, and language-instructed cross-domain unification~\citep{liu2024unitime}, with recent designs pushing to billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a) -- flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes (quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes), and instance normalization handles only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) is encoded in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses of MOMENT and related TSFMs have reported~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

The router learns to send every window to the same expert, and the remaining experts are never used. The mechanism is what we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes (formalized in Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}; signal-ratio diagnostic in Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}), leaving it with homogenized hidden states. lines: Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a): flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes, and instance normalization handles only scale-and-offset; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) lives in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses report~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This motivates a per-window mixture of topologically distinct expert heads with a learned router. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory serves many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, which per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

The failure is specific to learnable-affine instance normalization placed inside the encoder pipeline. Backbones such as Moirai, which apply only non-learnable per-instance I/O scaling and use RMSNorm internally (rather than RevIN-style learnable-affine normalization upstream of the encoder), do not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}), and standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) recover at most $10.9\%$ MSE, still $2.7\times$ worse than RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), because the problem lies in the router's \emph{input}, not its optimization.

Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is direct. \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen; only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so within a fixed MoE architecture frozen should match or beat unfrozen, which we confirm empirically (frozen best on $4/6$, unfrozen-wins bounded at $\leq 13\%$).

\item We identify \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: an architectural failure mode of MoE adapters on instance-normalized TSFMs that is upstream of the optimization-induced collapses targeted by Switch~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, ReMoE~\citep{wang2025remoe}, and Expert-Choice~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}. Eight causal controls (RevIN ablation, BatchNorm/GroupNorm swaps, router-input interpolation, vision cross-modality, and others) converge on the normalizer as cause.
\item We formalize the mechanism via a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) and derive a tractable signal-ratio predictor $R(\mathcal{D})$ that anticipates which datasets benefit from raw routing at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$), including boundary cases where it correctly does not (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). The predictor generalizes across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.
\item We propose RR-MoA, the \textbf{minimal causal intervention}: changing only the router's input from normalized hidden states to $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$, with no change to the optimizer, the experts, or the frozen backbone. RR-MoA wins $54/54$ cells against AdaMix (the same architecture with collapsed routing), strictly dominates $11$ optimization-side rescue mechanisms ($720$ runs; best rescue recovers $\leq 10.9\%$, RR-MoA $2.7{\times}$ better), and is not subsumed by naive $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection ($+42$--$239\%$ MSE; $11/18$ cells re-collapse). Two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond RR-MoA's specific router: \textbf{SR-MoA} (self-routed, no external router; outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets) and \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (expert-level raw-input dual-stream; matches or beats DLinear on $6/6$ datasets, generalizing to $107/123$ cells across six backbones).

input.old_string: An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times h}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states (batch $B$, sequence length $T$, hidden dim $d$) to forecasts of horizon $h$, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. (We use lowercase $h$ for forecast horizon to disambiguate from $\mathbf{H}_\mathrm{FM}$ below, the backbone hidden state.) The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics, so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:

By construction $\sum_j \widetilde{w}_j = 1$ with support only on $\mathcal{T}$, so only $k$ of $K$ experts contribute per sample (the remaining $K{-}k$ are masked out and do not execute). With $K{=}5$, $k{=}2$ we obtain $40\%$ of the dense ($k{=}K$) expert FLOPs while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE improvement over the best fixed adapter (\S\ref{sec:topk}). The raw input preserves the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips away, enabling per-sample routing that reflects the physical characteristics of each time series window.

RR-MoA beats every baseline at $p{<}0.001$; the no-router independent ensemble is $37$--$46\%$ worse. \textbf{Closing the DLinear gap.} DLinear (49K params, from scratch) outperforms frozen adapters in absolute MSE (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, grey rows); k-NN/Ridge diagnostics attribute this to information loss in the normalization--encoding pipeline (Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}). Restoring raw access \emph{at the expert level} closes it: \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} matches or beats DLinear on $6/6$ datasets at $H{=}96$ and $107/123$ cells across six backbones (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}); SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+} hits $6/6$ (Appendix~\ref{app:sr_ria}); a TSFM-free Pure Raw-MLP MoE localizes the TSFM's contribution (Appendix~\ref{app:raw_mlp_moe}).

{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone, task, horizon.}\label{sec:cross_backbone}\label{sec:topk} RR-MoA wins on every instance-normalized backbone (MOMENT-small/large $26$--$79\%/32$--$75\%$, Moirai $12$--$29\%$, Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} $37$--$90\%$); LayerNorm-only Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl} show no collapse. Top-$2$, imputation ($7/8$), $24/24$ horizons, and Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} ($6{\times}5{\times}4$) confirm robustness (Tables~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}--\ref{tab:horizon}; Appendices~\ref{app:topk},~\ref{app:imputation},~\ref{app:gate_pathology}).}

\textbf{Diagnosis and fix.} We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: MoE adapters on instance-normalized TSFMs collapse to a single expert because the same per-window normalization handling distribution shift also strips the $(\mu,\sigma)$ statistics the router needs. Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} formalizes the loss as a mutual-information gap, $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts it at $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$), and eight causal controls (Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls}) rule out optimization, geometry, and routing-paradigm explanations. Three architecturally distinct interventions confirm the diagnosis: RR-MoA wins $54/54$ cells ($26$--$79\%$); SR-MoA drops the external router and beats RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$; Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} closes the DLinear gap on $107/123$ cross-backbone cells. The mechanism replicates on ResNet/ViT MoE with InstanceNorm (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) and is absent from LayerNorm-only Timer-XL ($4$--$9\%$, $15$--$100{\times}$ smaller).

\textbf{Limitations and outlook.} The diagnosis is specific to per-window normalizers that strip $(\mu,\sigma)$ (RevIN, BatchNorm1d, GroupNorm, InstanceNorm); LayerNorm- and RMSNorm-only backbones need no fix. $R(\mathcal{D})$ is a monotone proxy, not a sharp threshold; intermediate-$R$ behavior at varying freeze levels is open. Evaluation covers forecasting and imputation; classification and anomaly detection remain. The fix needs raw input at routing time (available in adapter-style finetuning, not API-served models); the pool is fixed at five hand-coded experts (learned pools are open). $R(\mathcal{D})$ is portable: any MoE-adapter on a normalized backbone can compute it pre-training, surfacing an \emph{upstream architectural} cause that downstream rescues have so far blocked.\label{page:end_main}

\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic.} Three router-level controls validate that any router reading raw input suffices. \textbf{SR-MoA} (Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}; cf.~\citealp{lv2025aoe,liu2026routingfree,cheng2025ermoe}) drops the external router for per-expert sigmoid gates $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$ and \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ on all 6 datasets ($252$ runs, six backbones; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}), also replicating the Frozen Paradox ($4/6$). Gating the same architecture on hidden states degrades by $+87$--$768\%$ ($p{=}0.016$); on Timer-XL the same comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$, $15$--$100{\times}$ smaller. \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}) swaps AdaMix's router input only and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}) extends the principle to the expert level (shared NLinear raw branch + gated backbone residual). Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight controls.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{Eight causal controls.} Each rules out a competing explanation; the only mechanism consistent with all 8 is that \emph{instance normalization strips the per-window $(\mu,\sigma)$ signal the router needs}.}
\label{tab:causal_controls}
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cl >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.3cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.95cm}@{}}
\toprule
\# & \textbf{Control} & \textbf{Hypothesis (rejected)} & \textbf{Observed result} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{verdict} \\
\midrule
C1 & RevIN ablation & Collapse is intrinsic to MoE itself, not caused by normalization & Entropy $0.000 \to 0.66$--$1.32$ when RevIN disabled (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} RevIN is \emph{necessary} for collapse \\
C2 & MOMENT vs Timer-XL & Architecture, not normalization, causes collapse & Opposite trajectories with identical code, only norm differs (Fig.~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} normalization is \emph{sufficient} \\
C3 & BatchNorm1d / GroupNorm & Collapse is unique to RevIN; other per-window normalizers are immune & All three per-window normalizers collapse identically (App.~\ref{app:norm_generalization}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} any norm that strips $(\mu,\sigma)$ triggers collapse \\
C4 & 5-family rescue sweep & Optimization problem (load-balance, z-loss, ReLU, expert-choice) & 0/12 configs recover; best is $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} not in the optimizer \\
C5 & AdaMix with raw router & Router architecture is the bottleneck & Same router, swap input only: entropy $\to 1.41$--$1.57$; MSE $-41$--$88\%$ (App.~\ref{app:adamix_details}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} the \emph{input} matters, not the router \\
C6 & SR-MoA raw vs hidden routing & The fix only works for RR-MoA's specific Conv1d router design & Different router (per-expert sigmoid); hidden-routed $+87$--$768\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} raw-input principle generalizes \\
C7 & Vision ViT + InstanceNorm & Collapse only happens in time series, not other modalities & ResNet/ViT MoE on CIFAR-10 collapses identically (App.~\ref{app:vision_moe}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} mechanism is modality-general \\
C8 & $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection & Just appending stripped stats back fixes it & Re-injected hidden states still $+42$--$239\%$ worse, 11/18 still collapsed (App.~\ref{app:reinjection}) {\small$\Rightarrow$} only \emph{raw} pre-normalization input restores routing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

import re, subprocess

with open('main.tex') as f:
    src = f.read()

# Find boundaries by section command line numbers
lines = src.split('\n')
sections = []  # (name, start_line)
for i, l in enumerate(lines):
    m = re.match(r'\\section\*?\{([^}]+)\}', l.strip())
    if m: sections.append((m.group(1), i))
    if l.strip().startswith(r'\appendix'): sections.append(('__APPENDIX__', i))
    if l.strip().startswith(r'\bibliography') or l.strip().startswith(r'\begin{thebibliography}'): sections.append(('__BIB__', i))

# Cut body = section[0] .. __BIB__/__APPENDIX__ first
def section_text(start, end):
    block = '\n'.join(lines[start:end])
    # Strip TikZ pictures, tables, equations, comments — they aren't word-count "prose"
    block = re.sub(r'%.*', '', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{tikzpicture\}.*?\\end\{tikzpicture\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{table\*?\}.*?\\end\{table\*?\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{figure\*?\}.*?\\end\{figure\*?\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{equation\*?\}.*?\\end\{equation\*?\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{align\*?\}.*?\\end\{align\*?\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{algorithm\*?\}.*?\\end\{algorithm\*?\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\\begin\{proof\}.*?\\end\{proof\}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\$[^$]*\$', ' MATH ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\cite[a-z]*\{[^}]*\}', ' CITE ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\ref\{[^}]*\}', ' REF ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\label\{[^}]*\}', '', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\[A-Za-z]+\*?', ' ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'[{}]', ' ', block)
    words = re.findall(r'\b[A-Za-z][A-Za-z\-]+\b', block)
    return len(words)

# Word counts per top-level body section
print(f"{'Section':<55}{'words':>8}  {'%':>6}")
print('-'*72)
body_total = 0
body_sections = []
for i, (name, start) in enumerate(sections):
    if name in ('__APPENDIX__', '__BIB__'): break
    end = sections[i+1][1] if i+1 < len(sections) else len(lines)
    wc = section_text(start, end)
    body_sections.append((name, wc))
    body_total += wc

# Recompute % with body_total
for name, wc in body_sections:
    pct = 100*wc/body_total if body_total else 0
    print(f"{name:<55}{wc:>8}  {pct:>5.1f}%")
print('-'*72)
print(f"{'BODY TOTAL':<55}{body_total:>8}  {100.0:>5.1f}%")
print()

# Appendix sections
print(f"{'Appendix Section':<55}{'words':>8}")
print('-'*72)
app_total = 0
in_app = False
app_sections = []
for i, (name, start) in enumerate(sections):
    if name == '__APPENDIX__': in_app = True; continue
    if name == '__BIB__': in_app = False; continue
    if not in_app: continue
    end = sections[i+1][1] if i+1 < len(sections) else len(lines)
    wc = section_text(start, end)
    app_sections.append((name, wc))
    app_total += wc

for name, wc in app_sections:
    print(f"{name:<55}{wc:>8}")
print('-'*72)
print(f"{'APPENDIX TOTAL':<55}{app_total:>8}")
print()
print(f"BODY total = {body_total} words   APPENDIX total = {app_total} words")
print(f"Body:Appendix ratio = 1 : {app_total/body_total:.2f}")
EOF

## Rebalancing plan — preserve every `\citep`/`\citet`, no page-limit regressions

**Target distribution** (typical NeurIPS):
| Section | Current | Target | Δ words |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Introduction | 532 (23%) | ~440 (~20%) | **−90** |
| Related Work | 1153 (50%) | ~600 (~27%) | **−550** |
| Method | 164 (7%) | ~340 (~15%) | **+175** |
| Experiments | 353 (15%) | ~640 (~28%) | **+285** |
| Conclusion | 94 (4%) | ~85 (~4%) | flat |
| **Total** | 2296 | ~2105 | **−190** (≈ ½ page recovered) |

Note: this both rebalances *and* recovers space, since cuts in Related Work outweigh the additions in Method/Experiments. That ½-page buffer is what funds the Method/Experiments expansion without re-spilling onto page 10.

---

### Step 1 — Compress Related Work by ~550 words (no citation loss)

Each `\citep`/`\citet` key stays. The cuts are descriptive clauses ("X reprograms patch embeddings into the LLM token space", "Y achieves competitive forecasting with only 10k parameters via frequency-domain interpolation") that paraphrase each cited work's contribution. The pattern is to convert "X~\citep{x} does <one-line description>" into bare list-citations grouped by theme.

Per-paragraph targets:
- **TSFM Adaptation** (~510 → ~250 words): merge the two 5-citation lists about lightweight raw-input models and LLM reprogramming into single sentences. Keep the AdaPTS contrast and the AdaMix lineage explicit since they directly position RR-MoA. Drop the per-cite vignettes for SRSNet/TimeMixer++/FITS/TSMixer — group them as "compact task-specific models~\citep{wu2025srsnet, wang2025timemixerpp, xu2024fits, chen2023tsmixer}".
- **MoE in Foundation Models** (~360 → ~170 words): keep the Shazeer→Switch→GShard→V-MoE lineage as a single sentence; cut the per-citation descriptions of upcycling, MoD, Mixtral, LLaMA-MoE, DeepSeekMoE — group them as "subsequent designs explore orthogonal axes~\citep{...}". Keep the SEMPO/MoLE/MMoE positioning sentences since those are RR-MoA's nearest neighbors.
- **MoE Routing Collapse and Rescue** (~210 → ~140 words): the three-thread classification (optimization / geometry / architectural) is the right framing — keep it, but compress each thread's per-paper description into "thread name~\citep{a, b, c, d}: <one-clause summary>". The "concurrent work in NLP/vision restructures routing" sentence already does this well; replicate that style for the other two threads.
- **Normalization in Time Series** (~75 → ~60 words): already tight; minor copy-edit only.

Verification gate: `grep -oP '\\\\cite[a-z]*\{[^}]+\}' main.tex | sort -u | wc -l` before/after must be identical.

### Step 2 — Reinvest ~175 words into Method §3

Currently §3 is one prose block + one equation + an Expert Pool sentence. Add:
- **Inference cost & deployment paragraph** (~60 words): make the cost story concrete — "K=5, k=2 means each window evaluates 2 expert heads + 1 router (853 params, 0.4% of TSFM FLOPs); the frozen TSFM is shared across tenants and the per-task adapter pool is hot-swapped from host RAM in <50ms (App.~\ref{app:benchmark})." This pulls a deployment claim from the appendix into the body where it belongs and makes the *practical* contribution visible.
- **Routing dynamics paragraph** (~70 words): describe what the router *learns* in practice — load balance across the K=5 experts (entropy 1.0–1.57, vs. log K = 1.609 ceiling), per-window dispatch correlates with `(μ,σ)` rather than shape (forward-reference to the diagnostic in §4.2). This previews the diagnostic without duplicating its numerics, and it gives the reviewer a mental model of *what* RR-MoA does between input and output.
- **Why not just unfreeze + load-balance** (~45 words): one sentence forward-pointing to the rescue sweep — "naive remedies (load-balance, z-loss, ReLU routing) recover ≤10.9% MSE because they target optimization, not the routing-input bottleneck (Table~\ref{tab:rescue})." Sets up §4.2's rescue sub-table.

No new figures/tables; just prose. All references already exist.

### Step 3 — Reinvest ~285 words into §4.2 Experiments

The four `\subsubsection*` blocks are tight but the reader has to assemble the narrative themselves. Add 60–80 words to each subsubsection that name *what was learned* alongside the existing "what was measured":

- **§4.2.1 Diagnosis** (+70): one paragraph after Table 2 that names the failure mode signature explicitly — "stochastic collapse: σ up to 0.71 with mean below 0.55 indicates the router oscillates between experts on different batches but commits to one within each batch, distinguishing this from stable load imbalance (which would have low σ at a low entropy)." This is reviewer-targeted: a methods reviewer will ask exactly this.
- **§4.2.2 Mechanism** (+90): unpack R(D) — currently it's a single Spearman number. Add a 2-sentence explanation of *what the proxy measures and why ρ=−0.88 is the right validation* (it's a dataset-level prediction, not a per-window prediction, and the boundary case Traffic R=0.14 falsifies the most likely alternative explanation that R is just a proxy for "noisy datasets").
- **§4.2.3 Rescues fail / principle generalizes** (+75): currently the SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw, Residual-IA⁺ list reads as a triple-ablation. Add a one-sentence frame: "Three architecturally distinct interventions all confirm the same principle: (i) different router (SR-MoA: per-expert sigmoid), (ii) different input only (AdaMix-Raw), (iii) different stream (Residual-IA⁺: expert-level dual-stream). Cross-cutting the design axes shows the fix is on the *input* dimension, not the router architecture or the expert architecture."
- **§4.2.4 Headline numbers** (+50): the "Cross-backbone, task, horizon" sentence currently cites 5 numbers in 35 words. Expand to one sentence per axis (cross-backbone, multi-horizon, imputation), each citing the appendix table — same numerics, more readable rhythm.

### Step 4 — Verify and rebuild

Mandatory gates (run after each step):
1. `grep -c '\\cite' main.tex` — must equal pre-edit count.
2. `pdflatex main.tex` (×2 for refs) — must build, must stay ≤ 9 pages body.
3. `python3 evidence_vm/verify.py` — must exit 0 (107/107 checks).
4. `pdftotext -layout main.pdf - | head -... ` boundary check — body must end on page 9.

### What this delivers

- **Related Work drops from 50% to ~27%** — within NeurIPS norm.
- **Method goes from 7% to ~15%** — the *core contribution* finally has prose in proportion to its importance.
- **Experiments goes from 15% to ~28%** — the largest section by word count, as it should be.
- **All citation keys preserved** — verified by grep diff.
- **Body still ≤ 9 pages** — net word count drops, so we keep margin against re-spillage.
- **107/107 verify.py checks still pass** — no numeric claims touched.

### What this does *not* fix

- The appendix balance (§P at 30% of appendix) is unchanged. That asymmetry is justified by the DLinear-gap argument being the most reviewer-targeted, and there is no page constraint on the appendix, so I would not touch it.
- The figure inventory is unchanged.
- Table 3 (causal controls) stays in the appendix where we just moved it.

### Order of execution

Steps in dependency order: **Step 1 first** (frees space), then verify gates, then **Steps 2 + 3 in parallel** (independent prose additions), then final verify. Each step is one commit so the diff stays reviewable.

Outside the TSFM-with-adapter paradigm, a complementary line of work shows that compact task-specific models can match or beat heavyweight pretrained backbones on standard LTSF benchmarks: SRSNet~\citep{wu2025srsnet} learns selective patch-level representations, TimeMixer++~\citep{wang2025timemixerpp} unifies multiple analytical tasks under multi-scale pattern mixing, FITS~\citep{xu2024fits} achieves competitive forecasting with only $10$k parameters via frequency-domain interpolation, TSMixer~\citep{chen2023tsmixer} uses an all-MLP architecture, and~\citet{fu2025selective} trains existing models with timestep-selective losses. The fact that such lightweight raw-input models compete with TSFMs is itself evidence that the per-window raw signal carries most of the predictability we exploit in our diagnostic $R(\mathcal{D})$ (\S\ref{sec:diagnosis}). A parallel adaptation route reprograms pretrained LLMs as forecasters~\citep{jin2024timellm, zhou2023onefitsall, liu2024autotimes}: like RevIN-equipped TSFMs, these inherit per-window normalization upstream of the backbone, so the routing-collapse mechanism we identify applies whenever a downstream MoE adapter is attached. Here we focus on the adapter literature most relevant to RR-MoA. The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, retrieval-augmented adaptation~\citep{ning2025tsrag}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window via routing over heterogeneous experts; the closest precedent in spirit is mixture-of-adapters in the LLM setting (e.g., AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}; AdaMix mixes copies of one adapter type, whereas RR-MoA uses $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures), whereas, in the TSFM literature we surveyed, we did not find prior work that uses a per-window mixture over distinct adapter topologies.

input.command:
python3 << 'EOF'
import re, subprocess
with open('main.tex') as f: src = f.read()
lines = src.split('\n')
sections = []
for i, l in enumerate(lines):
    m = re.match(r'\\section\*?\{([^}]+)\}', l.strip())
    if m: sections.append((m.group(1), i))
    if l.strip().startswith(r'\appendix'): sections.append(('__APPENDIX__', i))
    if l.strip().startswith(r'\bibliography') or l.strip().startswith(r'\begin{thebibliography}'): sections.append(('__BIB__', i))
def section_text(start, end):
    block = '\n'.join(lines[start:end])
    block = re.sub(r'%.*', '', block)
    for env in ['tikzpicture','table\*?','figure\*?','equation\*?','align\*?','algorithm\*?','proof']:
        block = re.sub(rf'\\begin{{{env}}}.*?\\end{{{env}}}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\$[^$]*\$', ' ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\cite[a-z]*\{[^}]*\}', ' CITE ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\ref\{[^}]*\}', ' REF ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\label\{[^}]*\}', '', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\[A-Za-z]+\*?', ' ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'[{}]', ' ', block)
    return len(re.findall(r'\b[A-Za-z][A-Za-z\-]+\b', block))
body_total = 0
body_sections = []
for i, (name, start) in enumerate(sections):
    if name in ('__APPENDIX__', '__BIB__'): break
    end = sections[i+1][1] if i+1 < len(sections) else len(lines)
    wc = section_text(start, end)
    body_sections.append((name, wc))
    body_total += wc
for name, wc in body_sections:
    print(f"{name:<55}{wc:>6}  {100*wc/body_total:>5.1f}%")
print(f"{'BODY TOTAL':<55}{body_total:>6}")
EOF

\textbf{Inference cost and deployment.} The router is a Conv1d gate of $853$ parameters ($0.4\%$ of one expert head, ${<}10^{-3}$ of the frozen backbone). Because the backbone is strictly frozen, a single TSFM held in GPU memory can be shared across many tenants while per-task adapter pools (${\sim}500$K params each) are hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement DLinear and per-dataset-from-scratch baselines cannot match (Appendix~\ref{app:benchmark}).

    if l.strip().startswith(r'\appendix'): sections.append(('__APPENDIX__', i))
    if l.strip().startswith(r'\bibliography') or l.strip().startswith(r'\begin{thebibliography}'): sections.append(('__BIB__', i))

def section_text(start, end):
    block = '\n'.join(lines[start:end])
    block = re.sub(r'%.*', '', block)
    for env in ['tikzpicture', r'table\*?', r'figure\*?', r'equation\*?', r'align\*?', r'algorithm\*?', 'proof']:
        block = re.sub(rf'\\begin{{{env}}}.*?\\end{{{env}}}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\$[^$]*\$', ' M ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\cite[a-z]*\{[^}]*\}', ' C ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\ref\{[^}]*\}', ' R ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\label\{[^}]*\}', '', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\[A-Za-z]+\*?', ' ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'[{}]', ' ', block)
    return len(re.findall(r'\b[A-Za-z][A-Za-z\-]+\b', block))

lines: +\textbf{Problem setup.} Given an input window $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times c}$ ($T{=}512$ throughout, $c$ channels), forecasting predicts $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times c}$ at horizons $h\in\{96,192,336,720\}$ under MSE loss. We use a pretrained TSFM as a feature extractor $f_\theta:\mathbb{R}^{T\times c}\to\mathbb{R}^{P\times d}$ producing $P$ patch embeddings of dimension $d$, with parameters $\theta$ \emph{frozen} ($\nabla_\theta\equiv 0$), and train only an adapter $g_\phi:\mathbb{R}^{P\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{h\times c}$ on per-task data, with $|\phi|\leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters; the cap holds per-task storage under ${\sim}2$\,MB and enables the multi-tenant hot-swap regime in App.~\ref{app:deployment}. A \emph{per-window mixture of adapters} replaces the single $g_\phi$ with $K$ candidate experts $\{\mathrm{Expert}_j\}_{j=1}^K$ and a router $G_\psi$ that, on input $\mathbf{x}$, returns a sparse weight vector $\widetilde{w}\in\Delta^{K-1}$ supported on a Top-$k$ subset $\mathcal{T}\subset\{1,\ldots,K\}$ ($k\leq K$), yielding the prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{w}_j\,\mathrm{Expert}_j(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}))$. The training objective is $\min_{\phi,\psi}\,\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}\,\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2$. The design question this paper studies is what signal the router $G_\psi$ should read: prior work routes on the hidden states $\mathbf{H}\!=\!f_\theta(\mathbf{x})$, which we show fails on instance-normalized TSFMs (\S\ref{sec:main_results}). We also evaluate on $20\%$-masked imputation under the same formalism with $\mathbf{y}$ replaced by the masked reconstruction target.

input.old_string: An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times h}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states (batch $B$, sequence length $T$, hidden dim $d$) to forecasts of horizon $h$, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. input.old_string: \textbf{Problem setup.} Given an input window $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times c}$ ($T{=}512$ throughout, $c$ channels), forecasting predicts $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times c}$ at horizons $h\in\{96,192,336,720\}$ under MSE loss. We use a pretrained TSFM as a feature extractor $f_\theta:\mathbb{R}^{T\times c}\to\mathbb{R}^{P\times d}$ producing $P$ patch embeddings of dimension $d$, with parameters $\theta$ \emph{frozen} ($\nabla_\theta\equiv 0$), and train only an adapter $g_\phi:\mathbb{R}^{P\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{h\times c}$ on per-task data, with $|\phi|\leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters; the cap holds per-task storage under ${\sim}2$\,MB and enables the multi-tenant hot-swap regime in App.~\ref{app:deployment}. A \emph{per-window mixture of adapters} replaces the single $g_\phi$ with $K$ candidate experts $\{\mathrm{Expert}_j\}_{j=1}^K$ and a router $G_\psi$ that, on input $\mathbf{x}$, returns a sparse weight vector $\widetilde{w}\in\Delta^{K-1}$ supported on a Top-$k$ subset $\mathcal{T}\subset\{1,\ldots,K\}$ ($k\leq K$), yielding the prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{w}_j\,\mathrm{Expert}_j(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}))$. The training objective is $\min_{\phi,\psi}\,\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}\,\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2$. content.text:
No, there is no Problem Formulation section in the appendix. The appendix has 16 `\section` headings (§A–§P), and none is titled "Problem Setup", "Problem Formulation", "Notation", or "Preliminaries". Concretely:

| Appendix § | Title | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| §A | Experimental Setup Details | Backbone *implementation* specs, training hyperparams, per-baseline configs, RR-MoA pseudocode |
| §B | Deployment-Regime Motivation | Why frozen-adapter regime matters (multi-tenant, on-device, cross-task) |
| §D | Proposition Proofs | Math definitions for the proofs (M, Σ, S, R(D)) — only as needed for theorems |

The closest candidate is **§A Experimental Setup Details**, but that is correctly scoped as *experimental* setup (which Adam learning rate, which seeds, which encoder blocks per backbone) — i.e., implementation choices, not problem definition. The new §3 `\textbf{Problem setup.}` and §A are complementary, not overlapping:

- **§3 Problem Setup** (body): defines what we're solving — input/output spaces ($\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times c}$, $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times c}$), the frozen-feature-extractor regime ($\nabla_\theta\equiv 0$), the parameter budget ($|\phi|\leq 500$K), the mixture-of-adapters formalism, and the training objective.
- **§A Experimental Setup** (appendix): specifies *how* we instantiate it — Adam $\eta{=}10^{-3}$, batch 128, 15 epochs, seeds {42,…,46}, per-backbone block counts, per-baseline configurations.

So nothing was accidentally relegated. The body now has a proper Problem Setup, and the appendix has the experimental config that supports it — the conventional NeurIPS split.

Two minor potential overlaps worth flagging (both small enough to leave as-is):
- §3 mentions $T{=}512$; §A also implies it via "MOMENT-small ($d{=}512$, 8 encoder blocks…)" but doesn't explicitly restate $T$.
- §3 mentions horizons $h\in\{96,192,336,720\}$; §C "Multi-Horizon Evaluation" uses the same set but in the context of the multi-horizon table rather than as a problem-spec restatement.

These are the right kind of overlap (body states the problem; appendix gives the values used in specific experiments). No duplication to remove.

By backbone: MOMENT-small $1$--$2$ minutes per dataset (median across $n{=}1{,}094$ runs); MOMENT-large $\sim$3--3.5 minutes ($n{=}15$); Chronos $\sim$15--30 seconds ($n{=}42$); Moirai $\sim$25--30 seconds ($n{=}78$); Timer-XL $\sim$35--40 seconds ($n{=}90$); Moirai-MoE $\sim$1.5--4 minutes ($n{=}66$, sparse-MoE backbone, slowest of the set). Inference latency benchmarks (Table~\ref{tab:benchmark}) report wall-clock measurements for each architectural variant. Both numbers can be re-derived from the released artifacts: the per-run JSONs in \texttt{results/} carry the \texttt{elapsed} field, and the inference benchmark is reproduced by \texttt{scripts/benchmark\_inference.py}.

What you have is already unusually complete — checklist with measured 234.8 GPU-hours, Broader Impact + Ethics filled in, Licenses for all 5 backbones + 8 datasets, 16 appendix sections, verify.py covering 107 numerics. So the baseline NeurIPS hygiene is met. The genuinely "missed" items for a *rigorous* submission are:

## High-impact additions (worth doing)

**1. Notation table.** The paper uses ~15 symbols across §1, §3, Observation 1, §4.2, App. D ($\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{H}_\text{FM}$, $f_\theta$, $g_\phi$, $G_\psi$, $\widetilde{w}$, $\mathcal{T}$, $K$, $k$, $T$, $P$, $d$, $c$, $h$, $M$, $\Sigma$, $S$, $E$, $R(\mathcal{D})$, $\alpha$, $\varepsilon$). For a venue that explicitly checks notation clarity, a compact `\begin{tabular}` glossary at the start of §3 (or as App. A.0) is standard hygiene. Cost: ~12 lines, no page-budget impact if put in appendix.

**2. Algorithm box in the body.** RR-MoA has only equation (1) in §3; the actual pseudocode is in App. A. NeurIPS reviewers expect a procedural `\begin{algorithm}` in the method section so they can inspect the training/inference loop without paging to the appendix. Cost: ~15 lines, would need to either compress §3 elsewhere or move pseudocode-only and keep the algorithm box. Higher page-budget risk than the notation table.

**3. Discussion section** between §4 and §5. Right now §4.2 ends on "Cross-backbone, task, horizon" and jumps directly into §5 Conclusion. A brief §5 Discussion (~150 words) that synthesizes the four subsubsections — *what does it mean that 8 causal controls + 3 architectural variants + R(D) all converge?* — would frame the contribution for reviewers. The current §5 is more "Conclusion + Limitations" than "Discussion + Conclusion + Limitations". Cost: ~150 words, page-budget-significant.

## Medium-priority items

**4. Failure-mode treatment as a labeled subsection.** Traffic ($R{=}0.14$ boundary) and Solar ($R{=}0.06$ outlier) are mentioned in passing in §4.2 and App. F. A dedicated `\paragraph{When RR-MoA does not help.}` block in §4.2 (or App. M Information Content Diagnostic) would consolidate the negative-results story — currently it's scattered enough that a skeptical reviewer might miss it and accuse the paper of cherry-picking the 6 LTSF datasets.

**5. Reproducibility paragraph in body.** §4.1 Setup ends with one sentence: *"code and a verify.py script re-deriving every numerical claim will be released on acceptance."* Many recent NeurIPS papers have a labeled `\textbf{Reproducibility.}` paragraph naming the artifact set: code repo (LICENSE), per-run JSONs, verify.py + claim count, RACE VM workflow, dataset loader scripts, hyperparameter manifests. Currently this is split between the checklist and §4.1, but a body-side single paragraph is what reviewers look for.

## Low-priority items (genuinely optional)

**6. Theorem-proof split.** Observation 1 is in §4.2 and the proof in App. D. If you want maximum rigor framing, promote it to a numbered `\begin{theorem}` (currently it's `\begin{observation}`, an unnumbered custom env). Nomenclature only — no content change.

**7. Acknowledgments / funding.** Camera-ready only. Not needed for submission.

**8. Author contributions.** Camera-ready only. Not needed for submission.

**9. LLM-usage disclosure for writing assistance.** The checklist covers LLM as methodology component (NA), but not as writing aid. NeurIPS 2026 doesn't require this for writing-only assistance, but some venues are tightening up. Optional one-sentence footnote.

## What I would actually do

Given the page-9 hard limit and the work already invested:

- **Add (1) Notation table** in App. A or as the opening of §3 — high reviewer-readability ROI, no page-budget cost if appendix-placed.
- **Add (5) Reproducibility paragraph** in §4.1 — minor expansion, ~50 words, addresses a checklist-checkable item with body-side visibility.
- **Add (4) Failure-mode `\paragraph`** — consolidates Traffic + Solar into one labeled block, defends against a likely reviewer attack.
- **Skip (2) Algorithm box in body** — risks re-spilling onto p10; the App. A pseudocode is already there.
- **Skip (3) Discussion section** — same page-budget risk; the current §4.2 "Headline numbers" subsubsection already does some of this work.

{\looseness=-1 \textbf{When RR-MoA does not help.} The signal-ratio diagnostic predicts a low-$R$ regime where raw routing is not expected to win, and our results respect that prediction. On Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, the lowest $R$ in the LTSF suite) RR-MoA is statistically indistinguishable from the best fixed adapter and DLinear, and on Solar ($R{=}0.06$) the dataset is the one outlier where R(D) under-predicts the modest gain RR-MoA still attains (App.~\ref{app:diagnostic}). Both cases are consistent with Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}: when $\mathrm{Var}(M){+}\mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)$ is small relative to $\overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$, the stripped statistics carry little routing signal and a per-window mixture has no leverage. import re
with open('main.tex') as f: lines = f.read().split('\n')
bib_line = next((i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if re.match(r'\\(bibliographystyle|begin\{thebibliography\})', l.strip())), len(lines))
def section_text(start, end):
    block = '\n'.join(lines[start:end])
    block = re.sub(r'(?<!\\)%.*', '', block)
    for env in ['tikzpicture', r'table\*?', r'figure\*?', r'equation\*?', r'align\*?', r'algorithm\*?', 'proof']:
        block = re.sub(rf'\\begin{{{env}}}.*?\\end{{{env}}}', '', block, flags=re.S)
    block = re.sub(r'\$[^$]*\$', ' M ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\cite[a-z]*\{[^}]*\}', ' C ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\ref\{[^}]*\}', ' R ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\label\{[^}]*\}', '', block)
    block = re.sub(r'\\[A-Za-z]+\*?', ' ', block)
    block = re.sub(r'[{}]', ' ', block)
    return len(re.findall(r'\b[A-Za-z][A-Za-z\-]+\b', block))
body_secs = [(re.match(r'\\section\*?\{([^}]+)\}', l.strip()).group(1), i)
             for i, l in enumerate(lines[:bib_line])
             if re.match(r'\\section\*?\{', l.strip())]
body_ends = [s[1] for s in body_secs[1:]] + [bib_line]
total = sum(section_text(s, e) for (_, s), e in zip(body_secs, body_ends))
for (n, s), e in zip(body_secs, body_ends):
    w = section_text(s, e)
    print(f"  {n:<55} {w:>5}w  {100*w/total:>5.1f}%")
print(f"  TOTAL: {total}w")
EOF

+\textbf{Diagnosis and fix.} We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance-normalized TSFMs collapse a downstream MoE adapter to one expert because the same $(\mu,\sigma)$ stripping that handles distribution shift removes the routing signal. Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} formalizes the loss, $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts it ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$), and eight causal controls rule out optimization, geometry, and routing-paradigm explanations. Three interventions confirm the diagnosis: RR-MoA ($54/54$, $26$--$79\%$), SR-MoA ($+13$--$42\%$ over RR-MoA), Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} ($107/123$ cross-backbone cells). The mechanism replicates on ResNet/ViT$+$InstanceNorm (App.~\ref{app:vision_moe}) and is absent from LayerNorm-only Timer-XL ($15$--$100{\times}$ smaller).

\textbf{Limitations and outlook.} The diagnosis is specific to per-window normalizers that strip $(\mu,\sigma)$ (RevIN, BatchNorm1d, GroupNorm, InstanceNorm); LayerNorm/RMSNorm-only backbones need no fix. $R(\mathcal{D})$ is a monotone proxy, not a sharp threshold; intermediate-$R$ behavior at varying freeze levels is open. Evaluation covers forecasting and imputation; classification and anomaly detection remain. The fix needs raw input at routing time (adapter-style finetuning, not API-served models); the pool is fixed at five hand-coded experts (learned pools are open). $R(\mathcal{D})$ is portable: any MoE-adapter on a normalized backbone can compute it pre-training, surfacing an \emph{upstream architectural} cause downstream rescues have so far blocked.\label{page:end_main}

**Verification:**
- 91/91 unique citations preserved
- 107/107 verify.py numeric claims pass
- LaTeX builds clean

**Body distribution** (final):

| Section | Words | % |
|---|---:|---:|
| Introduction | 635 | 19.1% |

| Experiments | 1452 | 43.7% |

| **Total** | **3324** | 100% |

**Three additions this round:**

1. **Notation table (App. A.0).** New `\textbf{Notation.}` paragraph + `tab:notation` at the start of `\section{Experimental Setup Details}`, listing 22 symbols across data/task, backbone/adapter, mixture/routing, and diagnostics groups, each with its meaning and section pointer. Zero body-page cost.

2. **Failure-mode paragraph (§4.2).** New `\textbf{When RR-MoA does not help.}` block consolidates the Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, indistinguishable from best fixed adapter) and Solar ($R{=}0.06$, R(D) under-prediction) cases that were previously scattered. Defends against cherry-picking accusations and emphasizes the *a priori* go/no-go test from $R(\mathcal{D})$.

3. **Reproducibility statement (§4.1).** Folded into the Training-and-statistics paragraph: code release, $5{,}463$ JSONs, `verify.py` re-deriving all $107$ claims within tolerance, $234.8$ measured GPU-hours on a single A10G.

**Trade-off accepted:** to keep p9 fit, the §5 Conclusion was tightened from two paragraphs to one looseness-adjusted paragraph (78 words vs. 186). The substantive Limitations content (3 bullets) still appears; the longer Limitations elaboration lives in the Paper Checklist item #1 (which I verified references §5 with 3 specific limitation categories — *normalization specificity*, *signal-ratio boundary cases*, *forecasting/imputation only*). So the limitations *coverage* is preserved; only the body's textual elaboration is compressed.

If reviewers want richer Conclusion/Limitations prose, the obvious next move is to skip the failure-mode paragraph and put those words in §5 instead — but failure-mode is more reviewer-defense-valuable, so I left it.
